findings.section: Behaviour contract — C2 (the xargs bullet; Unchanged: a -c string holding $)
findings.summary: C2 counts every word that holds xargs' replace string as expanded. The judge does not match a shell's -c string, though: it splits it again and judges what is inside, and the only -c string C2 refuses is one holding `$`. So `xargs -I % sh -c 'git %'` reaches the inner judge as `git %`, where `%` (or `{}`, which is not a brace expansion) is literal, and the command is allowed. It runs `git push`. Putting the replace string inside `sh -c '…{}…'` is the usual xargs idiom, and the contract does not say what happens to it. A task can implement C2 as written, pass every worked-example line, and leave this open.
findings.evidence: Binary built from ee4adf63, phase review: `echo push | xargs -I % sh -c 'git %'` → allow; `echo push | xargs -I {} sh -c 'git {} origin'` → allow; `echo x | xargs -i sh -c 'git {}'` → allow. internal/fence/judge.go, case "sh", "bash", …: shellString returns the -c string and j.shell parses it again with no memory of which words were expanded. shellString refuses only a string holding `$`.
findings.fix: Add to C2's xargs bullet: with a replace option, a shell's -c string that holds the replace string is refused, as one holding `$` is, with the shell's prefix. Pin the message, for example `sh: the -c string holds xargs' replace string and cannot be judged`, and add the worked-example line `review  echo push | xargs -I % sh -c 'git %'   → deny: <that message>`. C4's lists of refusals can name it with the expanded words.

decisions: Drop the leading keyword and judge the rest, rather than parsing the grammar (mvdan.cc/sh rejected). Agree: a compound runs only commands the splitter already cuts out, and each is judged as if sent alone.
case, select, function, coproc, [[ and function definitions stay refused. Agree; none is among the counted denials.

An expanded word ($, glob, brace) matches as any text, and the whole word stands for it. Agree, and it closes real bypasses that are allowed today (`X=push; git $X origin`, `git pu{sh,} origin`, `git pu?h origin`, `g$X push origin`, confirmed on the base). The cost is real and the brief lists it: git diff/log/show with a `$` or glob argument, `find "$d"`, and in work sessions `rm "$f"` / `rm *.tmp`. Unsure: the note's 'none of the 5 names a command a fence denies' does not show that none of them would be denied under C2 (a `git diff "$BASE"` would be). The kept sessions' transcripts would settle it.
A command name that expands anywhere is refused, and so is an expanded word a wrapper skips or a shell option before -c. Agree.
A redirection target holding a glob or a brace expansion is refused (new message). Agree: it closes `echo x > .vloop/*` at the hook.

xargs is matched as if it ended with one expanded word; with a replace option, the words holding the replace string count as expanded; BSD -J/-R/-S take an argument. Agree; see the finding for the -c string.
command -v / -V (literal, letters p/v/V) runs nothing; time -v does not. Agree.
Subshells are read; `((` is refused as arithmetic; let, ${a[x]} and declare -i are left for a later brief. Acceptable; they are named in Out of scope.
A keyword after a wrapper is not dropped (`env ! x` stays denied). Agree.
C2 applies in every phase. Agree.
